title: The Riddle of the Laughing Clock
markdown:
Blackwood Junction kept an ancient disused platform, stone worn by travellers, moss like emerald velvet on crumbling brick. Time had forgotten it, except for a bench that had seen more sunsets than most people had birthdays. The air there had a habit of keeping secrets and then, at odd hours, of letting one slip.

Lila Bright came with a stout faded-leather notebook of unusual things. She never meant to poke. Her eyes and questions led her to the edge anyway. The current obsession: a small crisp note in elegant looping script, appearing on that same bench, decades apart, identical. Ink that smelled of lavender and regret. *The time to mend is nigh, when the tick-tock laughs a silent laugh.*

She had three copies now, or rather three appearances, pressed between blotting paper. Same words. Same lavender. Same faint crease as if the paper had been folded by the same impatient thumb. A joke that had outlived its audience. She had asked the stationmaster, who said benches did not write. She had asked the librarian, who offered a book on railway ghosts and looked disappointed when Lila wanted joke books instead. Pip, who had come for the ghosts, stayed for the lavender.

Pip Flutterwing was a doer, boundless, loyal, a spare shoelace and a polished pebble always in the satchel. Helpfulness sometimes landed wrong: baker’s dough rearranged into a startling star-shaped loaf that tasted of ginger; library books organised by colour, biographies lost among poetry. He squinted at the note. “A clock with a broken chime? A mouse trying not to wake a cat?”

“A joke from a time when people knew things we don’t,” Lila said. “A riddle wrapped in an enigma. A secret across years.”

Their investigation, curiosity and companionship, led to the hushed halls of the local museum, a grand old building with stone lions at the door, a trove of forgotten histories. Hours among faded photographs and crumbling letters. A stationmaster’s log that mentioned an unexplained mist on Platform Three in 1912, written in a hand that had tried to be official and failed at the word *mist*. A watchmaker’s advertisement promising *messages of a most particular punctuality*, the paper foxed, the promise still sharp. Pip dropped a pebble, picked it up, and apologised to a glass case that had not noticed. Amid historical artefacts, a small case of children’s joke books from the early 1900s. Titles enough to make Lila giggle, a rare sound: *Giggles Galore*, *Chuckles from the Century*, the particularly intriguing *Jest of the Ages*.

Pip, ever eager, nudged the display with his elbow. Clang. A small intricately carved wooden bird, once perched atop a grand grandfather clock, toppled and landed with a gentle thud, precisely on the open page of *Jest of the Ages*. The book lay as if waiting for this very moment.

A child’s bold round script: *What has a face, but no eyes? What has hands, but no arms? What laughs without a sound, when its purpose is found?* Faint pencil beneath: *A clock that tells its own time.*

Lila read it aloud. Air shimmered, the moment before a rainbow. The bird in Pip’s hand glowed, carved eyes catching a light that was not in the room. The platform, somehow, was under their feet again, though they had not walked there. The very air vibrated.

Blink. Same stones, newer. Coal smoke, horse-drawn carriages, top hats, long skirts. A boy selling papers shouted a headline about a king Lila had only met in history. Iron wheels complained in a key the modern junction had forgotten. Pip’s satchel, which had been modern a breath ago, looked suddenly like a thing that might be confiscated for being too odd. The note still on the bench, as if time had paused and resumed around them.

A man with kind weary eyes and ink-stained fingers approached, leather diary in hand. “You found it. The note. You understand the jest.”

This was Mr Alistair Finch, master watchmaker from the year 1912, clothes simple but finely made. Quiet genius whose passion for gears and springs bordered on obsession. He had been experimenting with a peculiar mechanism of his own invention, designed to send messages across time. The goal was ambitious: to guide his future self to a forgotten family heirloom that held a vital secret. *The tick-tock laughs a silent laugh* was his whimsical, heartfelt way of describing the moment his temporal message would be understood. He had intended the note for himself. A minor malfunction, a tiny spark of miscalculation, had caused it to echo through the years, appearing again and again on that lonely bench, a temporal ghost.

“My machine is unstable.” Brass, crystals, vacuum tubes on a reinforced trolley, wondrous and precarious, humming as if it had a headache. “The loop grows stronger. A prison. I may repeat the same day, the same hope, forever.” He wrung his hands. The diary’s pages were full of the same date.

Lila saw a loose wire, intermittent crimson flash. She never meant to interfere with another century’s work. She ventured anyway. “If we reroute this, just a little.”

Pip produced sturdy twine and, for once, tied a knot perfectly placed. He polished the wooden bird. It hummed, as if the joke had found its punchline and was waiting for someone to stop interrupting. Lila, following Alistair’s urgent whispers, made the delicate adjustment. A crystal that had been singing the wrong note settled. She had never meant to touch another century’s brass, and she touched it anyway, because a loose wire was a loose wire in any year. Pip’s shiny button caught the machine’s glow. The trolley stopped shivering. The diary, open on the bench, no longer needed the same date twice.

Alistair, watching, almost smiled. “I built it to speak to myself. It appears I required a better audience.”

A final resonant whirr, in the air and under it. The shimmer receded like a tide.

“You’ve stabilised it. The loop is broken. The message will be sent once, as intended.” His eyes were wet. “The timepiece of destiny is best understood by the young at heart, who still believe in a perfectly timed jest.”

The platform shimmered once more, this time with a gentle settling light, last rays on a tranquil evening. Coal smoke faded, replaced by old wood and faint damp, the scent of their own time. They were back. The note on the bench was gone, leaving no trace of its temporal journey. The wooden bird, ordinary again, sat in Lila’s palm, still slightly warm.

Alistair Finch was no longer in their century; his gratitude lingered like a warm room after someone has left. Lila closed the notebook on a blank page she did not fill with a moral. Pip tucked the twine away, proud of a knot that had landed right. The bench was only a bench. Blackwood Junction kept its moss and its secrets, and the next sunset, when it came, did not bring a note. Pip, later, organised nothing by colour. Lila, later, left one page empty on purpose, which was how you knew a joke had finished laughing.
characters: Lila Bright (girl who never means to break rules but somehow does), Pip Flutterwing (a friend who cannot stop making helpful mistakes)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic adventure story for older children
